entities.name: Guillaume d'Aure
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guillaume d'Aure, a prominent French Benedictine monk and prelate, rose to the influential position of Cardinal during the tumultuous Avignon Papacy, dying on 11 December 1353 in Avignon. Born into the powerful House of Comminges, as the son of Bernard VII Dodon, Count of Comminges, and Bertrande, Countess d'Aure, his aristocratic lineage provided a crucial foundation for his ecclesiastical ascent within the highly politicized medieval church. His career exemplifies the deep interweaving of noble power, monastic tradition, and papal authority in 14th-century Europe, particularly as the papacy navigated its relocation to Avignon.

His ecclesiastical career began with his profession as a Benedictine monk, leading to his appointment as Abbot of Montolieu. By 1342, he was consecrated Bishop of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières, a significant episcopal see in Languedoc. His elevation to the College of Cardinals by Pope Clement VI on 29 May 1342, with the title of Cardinal-Priest of Santo Stefano al Monte Celio, marked the zenith of his influence. As a cardinal, d'Aure became an integral part of the papal curia in Avignon, participating in the administrative and diplomatic functions of the church during a period characterized by political intrigue, the Black Death, and the Hundred Years' War.

Cardinal d'Aure's presence in the College of Cardinals contributed to the consolidation of French influence within the Avignon Papacy, a trend that shaped papal policy and appointments for decades. His family, the Counts of Comminges, further leveraged his position to maintain their own regional power and secure additional ecclesiastical preferments for other family members, illustrating the dynastic nature of church offices. His participation in the curia helped to manage the vast financial and spiritual machinery of the medieval church, leaving a legacy of administrative continuity during a period of significant upheaval.
